claim: Tomo-seq was used to establish a genome-wide expression dataset with high spatial resolution for the developing zebrafish heart at 2 days post-fertilization.
source: To obtain a transcriptome map of the developing heart at that stage with spatial resolution, we applied the tomo-seq method on dissected hearts from 2-day-old zebrafish embryos (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental method used and references Figure 1A showing the experimental design.

claim: The tomo-seq dataset contains expression information for approximately 13,000 genes.
source: We obtained a gene expression dataset with expression information for ~13,000 genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of genes detected and references supplementary data.

claim: Pearson's correlation analysis revealed blocks of continuous sections with high positive correlation of overall gene expression.
source: To assess global transcriptome patterns in the dataset, we implemented Pearson's correlation analysis, a pairwise measurement of linear correlation per section across the total transcriptome. Several blocks of continuous sections with high positive correlation of overall gene expression were observed (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the analysis method and Figure 1B shows the correlation heatmap.

claim: Hierarchical clustering analysis identified four large gene clusters with region-specific expression corresponding to the outflow tract, ventricle, AV canal and atrium.
source: The cluster plot confirmed the presence of four large gene clusters with region-specific expression, which likely corresponded to the outflow tract, ventricle, AV canal and atrium based on the genes present within these clusters (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the clustering results and Figure 1C shows the hierarchical cluster analysis.

claim: At 2 days post-fertilization, the zebrafish heart has developed into a looped structure with a recognizable atrium and ventricle that is able to sustain blood circulation.
source: At 2 days post-fertilization (2 dpf), the zebrafish heart has developed into a looped structure with a recognizable atrium and ventricle that is able to sustain blood circulation in the larvae.
evidence: This is a statement about zebrafish cardiac development that is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Functional Isl1+ pacemaker cells are located in the sinoatrial region at 2 days post-fertilization.
source: At this stage, functional Isl+ pacemaker cells are located in the sinoatrial region (Arrenberg et al., 2010; Tessadori et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous publications supporting this claim.

claim: Expression of myosin light chain 7 (myl7) defines the boundaries of the myocardial tissue.
source: Expression of myosin light chain 7 (myl7) defining the boundaries of the myocardial tissue (Figure 2A), indicated that all sections with exception of the first ten, were derived from myocardial tissue.
evidence: The manuscript describes myl7 expression pattern and Figure 2A shows the expression trace and in situ hybridization.

claim: Natriuretic peptide a (nppa) expression is restricted to the working myocardium of the ventricle and atrium and is absent from the non-working myocardium of the outflow tract, AV canal and SA region.
source: Natriuretic peptide a (nppa) expression is restricted to the working myocardium of the ventricle and atrium and was absent from the non-working myocardium of the outflow tract, AV canal and SA region (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript describes nppa expression pattern and Figure 2B shows the expression trace and in situ hybridization.

claim: Ventricle myosin heavy chain (vmhc) is specifically expressed in the ventricle.
source: Together with the ventricle-specific expression of ventricle myosin heavy chain (vmhc) (Figure 2C)
evidence: The manuscript describes vmhc expression and Figure 2C shows the expression trace and in situ hybridization.

claim: Atrial myosin heavy chain 6 (myh6) is specifically expressed in the atrium.
source: and atrial-specific myosin heavy chain 6 (myh6) (Figure 2D) we concluded that the ventricle and the atrium were well separated in the tomo-seq data.
evidence: The manuscript describes myh6 expression and Figure 2D shows the expression trace and in situ hybridization.

claim: Hyaluronan synthase 2 (has2) is expressed in the endocardial cushions of the outflow tract and AV canal.
source: To address whether genes that are expressed in the endocardial cushions, which give rise to the cardiac valves located in the outflow tract and in the AV canal, are present in the tomo-seq data, we analyzed the expression of hyaluronan synthase 2 (has2) (Figure 2E). Indeed, has2 was detected in the sections assigned to the outflow tract and the AV canal.
evidence: The manuscript describes has2 expression and Figure 2E shows the expression trace and in situ hybridization.

claim: Bone morphogenetic protein 4 (bmp4) and T-box protein 2b (tbx2b) are expressed in the non-working myocardium of the AV canal.
source: The non-working myocardium of the AV canal can be distinguished by the expression of bone morphogenetic protein 4 (bmp4) and T-box protein 2b (tbx2b). Both genes showed a peak expression around section 25, indicating the position of the AV myocardium (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: The manuscript describes bmp4 and tbx2b expression patterns and Figures 2F and 2G show the expression traces and in situ hybridizations.

claim: Bmp4 is also expressed in the SA region.
source: Importantly, bmp4 is also expressed in the SA region (Figure 2F). In the tomo-seq data, a clear expression peak was detected around section 34 (Figure 2F), indicating the position of the SA region in the tomo-seq data.
evidence: The manuscript describes bmp4 expression in the SA region and Figure 2F shows the expression trace and in situ hybridization.

claim: A total of 1143 genes were identified as differentially expressed in cardiac sub-compartments (ventricle, atrium, AV canal and sinoatrial region).
source: With this approach, we identified a total of 1143 genes for which their expression was upregulated in one of the selected cardiac sub-compartments (ventricle, atrium, AV canal and sinoatrial region) (log2 FC >2 and p<0.05) (Figure 4A–C and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript states the number of differentially expressed genes and references Figure 4 and source data.

claim: 99 genes were identified with upregulated expression in the atrium.
source: We identified 99 genes with upregulated expression in the atrium and 196 genes with upregulated expression in the ventricle (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript states the number of atrium-specific genes and references Figure 4A.

claim: 196 genes were identified with upregulated expression in the ventricle.
source: We identified 99 genes with upregulated expression in the atrium and 196 genes with upregulated expression in the ventricle (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript states the number of ventricle-specific genes and references Figure 4A.

claim: 346 genes were identified as differentially expressed in the AV canal.
source: We identified 346 differentially expressed genes in the AV canal, but gene-ontology analysis did not reveal any significant enrichment for specific biological processes.
evidence: The manuscript states the number of AV canal-specific genes.

claim: 502 genes were identified as differentially expressed in the sinoatrial region.
source: The sinoatrial region contains the pacemaker and proepicardial cells. The majority (502) of the sub-compartment-specific upregulated genes was identified in this region.
evidence: The manuscript states the number of sinoatrial region-specific genes.

claim: Gene ontology analysis revealed enrichment in oxygen transport and tricarboxylic acid cycle genes in the ventricle.
source: Gene ontology analysis revealed enrichment in oxygen transport and tricarboxylic acid cycle genes in the ventricle, suggesting that already in the 2-day-old ventricle metabolism is converting to aerobic oxidative phosphorylation to fulfill higher energy demands (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript describes GO term enrichment results and references Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The 2-day-old ventricle metabolism is converting to aerobic oxidative phosphorylation to fulfill higher energy demands.
source: Gene ontology analysis revealed enrichment in oxygen transport and tricarboxylic acid cycle genes in the ventricle, suggesting that already in the 2-day-old ventricle metabolism is converting to aerobic oxidative phosphorylation to fulfill higher energy demands (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the GO term enrichment data.

claim: Several genes related to cardiac myopathies were found amongst the ventricle specific genes.
source: Furthermore, several genes related to cardiac myopathies were found amongst the ventricle specific genes (e.g. csrp3, rcan1a (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), tnnc2, myo1c and actn1), indicating the value of the dataset for identifying potential disease-causing genes.
evidence: The manuscript identifies specific genes and references Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Gene ontology analysis revealed enrichment in proepicardium development genes in the sinoatrial region.
source: Gene ontology analysis revealed enrichment in proepicardium development genes based on differential expression of tbx5a, acvr1l and bmp4 in the sinoatrial region (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript describes GO term enrichment results and references Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Hippo signaling genes were enriched in the sinoatrial region.
source: In addition, several known regulators of pacemaker development (e.g. isl1 and shox2) were identified in our analysis (Figure 4C,F). Interestingly, hippo signaling genes were enriched in the gene ontology analysis. Indeed, the tomo-seq dataset contained several components of active hippo signaling, sav1, stk3 and lats1/2 that were differentially expressed in the sinoatrial region.
evidence: The manuscript describes GO term enrichment and identifies specific genes.

claim: Several components of the Wnt-signaling pathway were enriched in the sinoatrial region.
source: Moreover, we noticed that several components of the Wnt-signaling pathway were amongst the genes enriched in the sinoatrial region, such as casein kinase 1, alpha 1 (csnk1a1), frizzled homolog 2 (fzd2) and frizzled homolog 9b (fzd9b) (Figure 4C,F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript identifies specific Wnt pathway genes and references figures.

claim: Lymphatic vessel endothelial hyaluronic receptor 1a (lyve1a) is upregulated in the sinoatrial region.
source: Finally, the differential gene expression analysis identified lymphatic vessel endothelial hyaluronic receptor 1a (lyve1a) as being upregulated in the sinoatrial region.
evidence: The manuscript identifies lyve1a as differentially expressed.

claim: Factors associated with the lymphatic system (prox1a, prox1b, nr2f1a, nr2f2, elmo1 and foxj2) were expressed in the sinoatrial region.
source: Further factors associated with the lymphatic system were expressed in the sinoatrial region (prox1a, prox1b, nr2f1a, nr2f2, elmo1 and foxj2), suggesting that, as in the mammalian heart, cardiac lymphatics can develop from the sinus venosus (Klotz et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript identifies specific genes and cites a reference about mammalian cardiac lymphatics.

claim: Cardiac lymphatics can develop from the sinus venosus in zebrafish, as in the mammalian heart.
source: Further factors associated with the lymphatic system were expressed in the sinoatrial region (prox1a, prox1b, nr2f1a, nr2f2, elmo1 and foxj2), suggesting that, as in the mammalian heart, cardiac lymphatics can develop from the sinus venosus (Klotz et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from gene expression data and cites a reference about mammalian hearts.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling plays multiple roles during cardiac development.
source: Wnt ligands bind to Frizzled (Fzd) receptors to activate intracellular β-catenin signaling, which plays multiple roles during cardiac development (reviewed in [Gessert and Kühl, 2010]).
evidence: The manuscript cites a review article.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling has either positive or negative effects on cardiomyocyte differentiation depending on the developmental stage.
source: Depending on the developmental stage, Wnt/β-catenin signaling has either positive or negative effects on cardiomyocyte differentiation (Tzahor, 2007; Gessert and Kühl, 2010; Ueno et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references supporting this claim.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling in the atrioventricular canal induces the formation of endocardial cushions.
source: In addition, Wnt/β-catenin signaling in the atrioventricular (AV) canal induces the formation of endocardial cushions, giving rise to the AV valves, and the electrophysiological properties of the AV canal myocardium by slowing down electrical conductivity (Hurlstone et al., 2003; Verhoeven et al., 2011; Gillers et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references supporting this claim.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling in the atrioventricular canal regulates the electrophysiological properties of the AV canal myocardium by slowing down electrical conductivity.
source: In addition, Wnt/β-catenin signaling in the atrioventricular (AV) canal induces the formation of endocardial cushions, giving rise to the AV valves, and the electrophysiological properties of the AV canal myocardium by slowing down electrical conductivity (Hurlstone et al., 2003; Verhoeven et al., 2011; Gillers et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references supporting this claim.

claim: A role for Wnt/β-catenin signaling in pacemaker development has not been reported prior to this study.
source: Even though Wnt/β-catenin signaling has been studied extensively in the heart, a role in pacemaker development has not been reported.
evidence: The manuscript states this as background information.

claim: The Wnt receptor fzd9b is expressed in the sinoatrial region.
source: Expression of the Wnt receptor fzd9b was detected in sections 33–39 and whole mount in situ hybridization confirmed its expression in the sinoatrial region (Figure 4F).
evidence: The manuscript describes fzd9b expression and references Figure 4F showing expression trace and in situ hybridization.

claim: Expression of the Wnt inhibitor apcdd1l is observed in the atrium but is absent from the sinoatrial region.
source: In addition, expression of the Wnt inhibitor apcdd1l was observed in the atrium, but its expression was absent from sections 33 to 39, defining the sinoatrial region (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript describes apcdd1l expression pattern and references Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Wnt signaling is locally activated in the sinoatrial region.
source: From these results, we hypothesized that Wnt signaling is locally activated in the sinoatrial region.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a hypothesis based on gene expression data.

claim: Cells co-expressing TCF:mCherry reporter and Isl1:GFP reporter are located in the sinoatrial region.
source: Corroborating the hypothesis that Wnt/β-catenin signaling is activated in the sinoatrial junction, we observed cells that co-expressed both the TCF:mCherry reporter as well as the Isl1:GFP reporter in the sinoatrial region (Figure 5A–D').
evidence: The manuscript describes the observation and references Figure 5 showing confocal images.

claim: TCF-mCherry-positive cells are located in the AV canal.
source: In addition, TCF-mCherry-positive cells were also located in the AV canal, a cardiac sub-domain in which Wnt-signaling plays a known role (Gillers et al., 2015; Hurlstone et al., 2003; Verhoeven et al., 2011) (Figure 5C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the observation, cites references, and references Figure 5C.

claim: Wnt-signaling is activated in the Isl1+ cardiac pacemaker cells.
source: Thus, Wnt-signaling is activated in the Isl1+ cardiac pacemaker cells.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this from the co-expression data.

claim: Zebrafish embryos lacking functional Isl1 exhibit progressive failure of pacemaker function leading to severe bradycardia and arrhythmia.
source: In both zebrafish and mouse embryos lacking functional Isl1, a progressive failure of pacemaker function leads to severe bradycardia and arrhythmia (de Pater et al., 2009; Tessadori et al., 2012; Liang et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references supporting this claim.

claim: Mouse embryos lacking functional Isl1 exhibit progressive failure of pacemaker function leading to severe bradycardia and arrhythmia.
source: In both zebrafish and mouse embryos lacking functional Isl1, a progressive failure of pacemaker function leads to severe bradycardia and arrhythmia (de Pater et al., 2009; Tessadori et al., 2012; Liang et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references supporting this claim.

claim: Isl1-GFP+ cells are still present in the sinoatrial region of isl1 mutants.
source: Isl1-GFP+ cells were still present in the sinoatrial region of isl1 mutants (Figure 5A–B' and E–F'), suggesting that pacemaker cell specification still occurs in the absence of Isl1, but that these cells fail to differentiate into functional pacemaker cells.
evidence: The manuscript describes the observation and references Figure 5.

claim: Pacemaker cell specification still occurs in the absence of Isl1, but these cells fail to differentiate into functional pacemaker cells.
source: Isl1-GFP+ cells were still present in the sinoatrial region of isl1 mutants (Figure 5A–B' and E–F'), suggesting that pacemaker cell specification still occurs in the absence of Isl1, but that these cells fail to differentiate into functional pacemaker cells.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the presence of Isl1-GFP+ cells in mutants.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin activity is lost specifically in the Isl1-GFP+ cells of isl1 mutant embryos.
source: Interestingly, Wnt/β-catenin activity was lost specifically in the Isl1-GFP+ cells of the isl1 mutant embryos, while it was still detectable in the AV canal (Figure 5C,C', G and G').
evidence: The manuscript describes the observation and references Figure 5.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin activity is still detectable in the AV canal of isl1 mutant embryos.
source: Interestingly, Wnt/β-catenin activity was lost specifically in the Isl1-GFP+ cells of the isl1 mutant embryos, while it was still detectable in the AV canal (Figure 5C,C', G and G').
evidence: The manuscript describes the observation and references Figure 5.

claim: Active Wnt/β-catenin signaling in developing pacemaker cells depends on Isl1 activity.
source: These results reveal that in developing pacemaker cells active Wnt/β-catenin signaling depends on Isl1 activity.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this from the loss of Wnt activity in isl1 mutants.

claim: Inhibiting Wnt/β-catenin signaling by induction of Axin1 expression in the myocardium significantly increased cardiac contraction rates at 3 dpf.
source: Surprisingly and in contrast to the decreased heart rates observed in isl1-/- mutants (Tessadori et al., 2012; de Pater et al., 2009), inhibiting Wnt/β-catenin signaling by induction of Axin1 expression in the myocardium significantly increased cardiac contraction rates at 3 dpf (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental result and references Figure 6B,C.

claim: Despite the 10–15% increase in heart rate after Axin1 overexpression, the beating pattern was still regular.
source: Despite the 10–15% increase in heart rate, the beating pattern was still regular (see Figure 6—video 1 and Figure 6—video 2, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the observation and references videos and supplementary figure.

claim: Axin1 overexpression specifically between 36 hpf and 52 hpf significantly increased heart rate at 3 dpf.
source: Only Axin1 overexpression specifically between 36 hpf and 52 hpf, when the TCF:mCherry reported active Wnt signaling in the pacemaker cells, significantly increased heart rate (Figure 6D).
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal requirement and references Figure 6D.

claim: The M2 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor is expressed in the zebrafish heart from 30 hpf onwards.
source: The M2 mAChR is expressed in the zebrafish heart from 30 hpf onwards and by 3dpf the autonomic response is mature (Hsieh and Liao, 2002; Dlugos and Rabin, 2010; Shin et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references supporting this claim.

claim: By 3 dpf the autonomic response in the zebrafish heart is mature.
source: The M2 mAChR is expressed in the zebrafish heart from 30 hpf onwards and by 3dpf the autonomic response is mature (Hsieh and Liao, 2002; Dlugos and Rabin, 2010; Shin et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references supporting this claim.

claim: Control embryos showed a significant reduction in heart rate after addition of carbachol.
source: While control embryos showed a significant reduction in heart rate after addition of carbachol, the reduction in heart rate was abolished in Axin1 overexpressing embryos (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental result and references Figure 6E-F.

claim: The reduction in heart rate after carbachol treatment was abolished in Axin1 overexpressing embryos.
source: While control embryos showed a significant reduction in heart rate after addition of carbachol, the reduction in heart rate was abolished in Axin1 overexpressing embryos (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental result and references Figure 6E-F.

claim: Axin1-overexpressing embryos still responded to isoproterenol by increasing their heart rate.
source: Despite their already high heart rate, the Axin1-overexpressing embryos still responded to isoproterenol by increasing their heart rate further (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental result and references Figure 6E-F.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling in the heart regulates the parasympathetic, but not the sympathetic control of heart rate.
source: Together, these results indicate that Wnt/β-catenin signaling in the heart regulates the parasympathetic, but not the sympathetic control of heart rate.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this from the differential responses to carbachol and isoproterenol.

claim: At the examined embryonic stage, the heart lacks any direct innervation by the nervous system.
source: At the examined embryonic stage, the heart still lacks any direct innervation by the nervous system (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript states this and references Figure 6—figure supplement 2 showing immunohistochemistry.

claim: Muscarinic cholinergic receptor 2a (chrm2a) is expressed in the sinoatrial region of the adult zebrafish heart.
source: However, muscarinic cholinergic receptor 2a (chrm2a) encoding for the muscarinic M2 receptor responsible for parasympathetic regulation of the heart rate is expressed in the sinoatrial region of the adult zebrafish heart (Stoyek et al., 2016) as well as the embryonic heart (Steele et al., 2009; Thisse et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites references supporting this claim.

claim: Muscarinic cholinergic receptor 2a (chrm2a) is expressed in the embryonic zebrafish heart.
source: However, muscarinic cholinergic receptor 2a (chrm2a) encoding for the muscarinic M2 receptor responsible for parasympathetic regulation of the heart rate is expressed in the sinoatrial region of the adult zebrafish heart (Stoyek et al., 2016) as well as the embryonic heart (Steele et al., 2009; Thisse et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites references supporting this claim.

claim: At 2 and 3 dpf, chrm2a was expressed in the sinoatrial region of the heart.
source: At 2 and 3 dpf, chrm2a was expressed in the sinoatrial region of the heart (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the observation and references Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Overexpression of Axin1 resulted in a slight reduction in the expression of chrm2a.
source: Overexpression of Axin1 resulted in a slight reduction in the expression of chrm2a (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C), indicating that Wnt/β-catenin can work at the level of the M2 receptor.
evidence: The manuscript describes the observation and references Figure 6—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling can work at the level of the M2 receptor.
source: Overexpression of Axin1 resulted in a slight reduction in the expression of chrm2a (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C), indicating that Wnt/β-catenin can work at the level of the M2 receptor.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the reduction in chrm2a expression.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling plays a role in the autonomic control of heart rate by regulating pacemaker cellular response to parasympathetic stimuli.
source: Together, our results reveal a new role for Wnt/β-catenin signaling in the autonomic control of heart rate by regulating the response of pacemaker cells to parasympathetic stimuli (Figure 6G).
evidence: The manuscript concludes this from the experimental results and presents a model in Figure 6G.

claim: Cardiac pacemaker cells generate rhythmic action potentials through the combined and oscillating activity of ion channels on the surface membrane and calcium channels on the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
source: The cardiac pacemaker generates rhythmic action potentials through the combined and oscillating activity of ion channels on the surface membrane and calcium channels on the sarcoplasmic reticulum (Lakatta et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference supporting this claim.

claim: Heart rate can vary greatly in response to physiological demand, which is regulated by the autonomic nervous system.
source: Heart rate can vary greatly in response to physiological demand, which is regulated by the autonomic nervous system (Gordan et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference supporting this claim.

claim: In the adult zebrafish heart, the receptors enabling autonomic regulation are expressed in the Isl1+ pacemaker cells.
source: In the adult zebrafish heart, the receptors enabling autonomic regulation are expressed in the Isl1+ pacemaker cells (Stoyek et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference supporting this claim.

claim: Pacemaker cells are situated within, and coupled to, the surrounding cardiomyocytes, but retain a primitive myocardial identity.
source: Although pacemaker cells are situated within, and coupled to, the surrounding cardiomyocytes, they retain a primitive myocardial identity (Bakker et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference supporting this claim.

claim: During cardiac development, a myocardial progenitor cell population (Shox2+/Tbx18+/Isl1+/Nkx2.5-) becomes spatially restricted to the region connecting the sinus venosus to the atria (sinoatrial region).
source: This is established during cardiac development, when a myocardial progenitor cell population (Shox2+/Tbx18+/Isl1+/Nkx2.5-) becomes spatially restricted to the region connecting the sinus venosus to the atria (sinoatrial region).
evidence: The manuscript describes established knowledge about pacemaker development.

claim: Myocardial progenitor cells in the sinoatrial region differentiate into Isl1+/Hcn4+ pacemaker cells, strictly separated from the Nkx2.5+ working cardiomyocytes.
source: These progenitor cells differentiate into Isl1+/Hcn4+ pacemaker cells, strictly separated from the Nkx2.5+ working cardiomyocytes (Ye et al., 2015; Mommersteeg et al., 2007; Wiese et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references supporting this claim.

claim: Pacemaker cells are prevented from differentiating into working myocardium by Shox2, which inhibits Nkx2.5 expression.
source: The pacemaker cells are prevented from differentiating into working myocardium by Shox2, which inhibits Nkx2.5 expression (Espinoza-Lewis et al., 2011; Ye et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references supporting this claim.

claim: Isl1 plays a conserved role in pacemaker cells.
source: Isl1 plays a conserved role in pacemaker cells since zebrafish and mouse embryos lacking Isl1 have severe bradycardia progressing to complete loss of pacemaker function (de Pater et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2015; Tessadori et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple references supporting this claim.

claim: The etiology of the pacemaker phenotype in isl1 mutants is unclear.
source: The etiology of the pacemaker phenotype is unclear and mechanisms acting downstream of Isl1 to control heart rate remain to be determined.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a knowledge gap.

claim: Mechanisms acting downstream of Isl1 to control heart rate remain to be determined.
source: The etiology of the pacemaker phenotype is unclear and mechanisms acting downstream of Isl1 to control heart rate remain to be determined.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a knowledge gap.

claim: Electronic pacemakers can cause cardiac complications such as infections, recurring need for surgery to replace malfunctioning parts and the lack of autonomic responsiveness.
source: However, this is not ideal as electronic pacemakers can cause cardiac complications such as infections, recurring need for surgery to replace malfunctioning parts and the lack of autonomic responsiveness.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge about electronic pacemakers.

claim: Electronic pacemakers are not ideal for pediatric patients due to the continuous need to adapt the implanted device to the growing heart.
source: Furthermore, they are not ideal for pediatric patients due to the continuous need to adapt the implanted device to the growing heart.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge about electronic pacemakers.

claim: Biological pacemakers, generated in- or ex vivo, are being explored as alternatives to electronic pacemakers.
source: Biological pacemakers, generated in- or ex vivo are thus being explored as alternatives (Rosen et al., 2011; Protze et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites references supporting this claim.

claim: Generating biological pacemakers requires exquisite knowledge of the regulatory network driving pacemaker cell differentiation and function.
source: This, however, requires exquisite knowledge of the regulatory network driving pacemaker cell differentiation and function.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a logical requirement.

claim: Tomo-seq combines standard RNA-sequencing using barcoded primers with histological tissue dissection.
source: Tomo-seq combines standard RNA-sequencing using barcoded primers with histological tissue dissection and has been used to establish genome-wide transcriptome datasets with high spatial resolution of the whole zebrafish embryo and the injured adult zebrafish heart (Junker et al., 2014; Kruse et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites references describing the tomo-seq method.

claim: Tomo-seq has been used to establish genome-wide transcriptome datasets with high spatial resolution of the whole zebrafish embryo and the injured adult zebrafish heart.
source: Tomo-seq combines standard RNA-sequencing using barcoded primers with histological tissue dissection and has been used to establish genome-wide transcriptome datasets with high spatial resolution of the whole zebrafish embryo and the injured adult zebrafish heart (Junker et al., 2014; Kruse et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites references describing previous applications of tomo-seq.

claim: FISSEQ and tomo-seq techniques do not require prior anatomical annotation of the tissue.
source: The advantages of the FISSEQ and tomo-seq techniques compared to other mRNA-seq related techniques are that: (1) there is no need for prior anatomical annotation of the tissue
evidence: The manuscript states this as an advantage of these techniques.

claim: FISSEQ and tomo-seq techniques do not rely on tissue dissociation and cell sorting that can influence gene expression.
source: (2) it does not rely on tissue dissociation and cell sorting that can influence gene expression
evidence: The manuscript states this as an advantage of these techniques.

claim: FISSEQ and tomo-seq techniques maintain spatial information of the transcripts within the tissue.
source: (3) spatial information of the transcripts within the tissue is maintained.
evidence: The manuscript states this as an advantage of these techniques.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling in the AV canal regulates the expression of bmp4 and tbx2.
source: Wnt/β-catenin signaling in the AV canal regulates the expression of bmp4 and tbx2 (Verhoeven et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference supporting this claim.

claim: Expression of bmp4 and tbx2 in the sinoatrial region does not depend on Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
source: Although bmp4 and tbx2 are also expressed in the sinoatrial region, this expression does not depend on Wnt/β-catenin signaling ([Verhoeven et al., 2011] and data not shown).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference and mentions unpublished data.

claim: Isl1 is required for the activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling in the sinoatrial region.
source: We found that Isl1 is required for the activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling in the sinoatrial region (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Isl1 is not expressed in the AV canal.
source: Since isl1 is not expressed in the AV canal (Hami et al., 2011; Tessadori et al., 2012)
evidence: The manuscript cites references supporting this claim.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling plays different roles in the AV canal and sinoatrial region.
source: we conclude that Wnt/β-catenin signaling plays different roles in the AV canal and sinoatrial region.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this from the differential regulation of Wnt signaling in these regions.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling activity is required between 36 hpf and 52 hpf to reduce the heart rate.
source: We found that Wnt/β-catenin signaling activity is required between 36 hpf and 52 hpf to reduce the heart rate (Figure 6D).
evidence: The manuscript states this conclusion based on data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Isl1 has a central role in establishing pacemaker cell differentiation.
source: To explain these seemingly contradicting observations we propose a model in which Isl1 has a very central role in establishing pacemaker cell differentiation, while Wnt has a more specific downstream role during pacemaker function (Figure 6G).
evidence: The manuscript proposes this model and references Figure 6G.

claim: Wnt has a more specific downstream role during pacemaker function.
source: To explain these seemingly contradicting observations we propose a model in which Isl1 has a very central role in establishing pacemaker cell differentiation, while Wnt has a more specific downstream role during pacemaker function (Figure 6G).
evidence: The manuscript proposes this model and references Figure 6G.

claim: Isl1 regulates the expression of factors that are essential to drive the rhythmic membrane depolarizations specific for pacemaker cells.
source: We hypothesize that Isl1 regulates the expression of factors that are essential to drive the rhythmic membrane depolarizations, which is specific for pacemaker cells and absent from atrial cardiomyocytes.

claim: Without Isl1, the heart beat is maintained at low frequency because embryonic cardiomyocytes are able to spontaneously depolarize their membrane and contract.
source: Without Isl1 the heart beat is maintained at low frequency since embryonic cardiomyocytes are able to spontaneously depolarize their membrane and contract, explaining the low beating frequency observed in isl1-/- mutants (de Pater et al., 2009; Tessadori et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript proposes this explanation and cites references.

claim: When cardiomyocytes mature and lose their ability to spontaneously contract, the heartbeat of isl1-/- mutants stops.
source: When the cardiomyocytes mature, and lose their ability to spontaneously contract, the heartbeat of isl1-/- mutants stops since the rhythmic membrane depolarizations were not established.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this explanation.

claim: Isl1 induces Wnt/β-catenin signaling in the pacemaker cells to establish parasympathetic control of the rhythmic membrane depolarizations.
source: In addition, Isl1 induces Wnt/β-catenin signaling in the pacemaker cells to establish parasympathetic control of the rhythmic membrane depolarizations.

claim: Parasympathetic input through acetylcholine and muscarinic cholinergic receptors decreases the heart rate.
source: Since parasympathetic input through acetylcholine and muscarinic cholinergic receptors (mAChRs) decreases the heart rate, an increase in heart rate was observed after inhibiting Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge.

claim: Carbachol was unable to reduce heart rate in embryos in which Wnt/β-catenin signaling was inhibited.
source: Furthermore, we observed that carbachol, an acetylcholine agonist, was unable to reduce heart rate in embryos in which Wnt/β-catenin signaling was inhibited, indicating regulation at the level of the receptor or of downstream signaling.
evidence: The manuscript describes this observation and infers the mechanism.
